gloss: To make a person or a system seriously weak.
examples: Long hospital stays *debilitate* even young patients.
The infection *debilitated* him for months.
She was *debilitated* by the treatment, not by the disease itself.

gloss: To take money out of a bank account.
examples: The gym will *debit* your account on the first of every month.
They *debited* the full amount twice by mistake.
The fee has already been *debited*.
contrast: One t: *debited*, *debiting* — the stress is on DEB-. The opposite of *credit*.

gloss: To take the bones out of meat or fish before cooking.
examples: Ask the butcher to *debone* the chicken thighs.
He *deboned* the trout in about a minute.
The fillets come already *deboned*.

gloss: To show that a popular belief or claim is false.
examples: Nutritionists *debunk* this diet myth every January.
The reporter *debunked* the story in one afternoon.
That theory has been *debunked* many times over.

gloss: To remove most of the caffeine from coffee or tea.
examples: They *decaffeinate* the beans with water instead of chemicals.
The company *decaffeinated* its whole house blend.
I only drink *decaffeinated* coffee after six.

ru: внезапно уезжать, перебираться; сниматься с места
gloss: To leave a place suddenly, usually for somewhere better.
examples: Every August half the office *decamps* to the coast.
The band *decamped* to Nashville to record.
Fans were already *decamping* to the parking lot in the eighth inning.

gloss: To pour liquid slowly from one container into another, leaving the sediment behind.
examples: Let the wine breathe, or *decant* it into a pitcher.
She *decanted* the soup into three jars.
The oil is *decanted* into smaller bottles for the table.

gloss: To cut off the head of a person or an animal.
examples: Vandals *decapitate* the garden statues almost every spring.
The hailstorm *decapitated* every sunflower in the row.
The bronze figure had been *decapitated* sometime in the 1800s.

transitivity: both — transitive (*decarbonize* the grid), intransitive (heavy industry must *decarbonize*)
gloss: To cut the carbon emissions of an industry, a building, or a country to nearly zero.
examples: The plan is to *decarbonize* the power grid by 2035.
Steelmakers *decarbonized* faster than anyone expected.
Shipping is *decarbonizing* more slowly than aviation.

gloss: To slow down, or to make something slow down.
examples: Loaded trucks *decelerate* slowly on wet pavement.
Inflation *decelerated* for the fourth month in a row.
The train was *decelerating* as it entered the tunnel.

transitivity: both — transitive (*decentralize* the agency), intransitive (the network *decentralized*)
gloss: To move power or operations away from one central place to many smaller ones.
examples: The reform would *decentralize* hiring to individual schools.
The company *decentralized* its support teams last year.
Health care has been steadily *decentralized* since the 1990s.

gloss: To officially take away a license, an accreditation, or a union's recognition.
examples: The state can *decertify* an officer who lies under oath.
Regulators *decertified* two nursing homes in the county.
The union was *decertified* after a very close vote.
contrast: Consonant + *-y* changes: *decertifies*, *decertified*, but *decertifying* keeps the y.

gloss: To destroy a large part of a group or a population.
examples: Two bad winters can *decimate* a bee colony.
The layoffs *decimated* the newsroom.
Whole villages had been *decimated* by the epidemic.

gloss: To knock someone to the ground with a punch.
examples: One more word and I'll *deck* him.
He *decked* the guy in front of the whole bar.
The catcher got *decked* at home plate.
contrast: Informal. Not the same as the phrasal *deck out*, which means to decorate.

gloss: To remove the secret status from official documents so that the public can read them.
examples: Agencies *declassify* thousands of pages every year.
The White House *declassified* the memo on a Friday.
The cables were *declassified* thirty years later.

gloss: To remove an animal's claws, or to take the force out of something.
examples: Most American vets now refuse to *declaw* cats.
Amendments *declawed* the bill before the final vote.
The agency has been *declawed* by three rounds of budget cuts.

gloss: To free a country from colonial rule, or to strip colonial assumptions out of a subject.
examples: Britain began to *decolonize* Africa after the war.
Ghana was *decolonized* in 1957.
Several universities are *decolonizing* their reading lists.

gloss: To take a ship, a power plant, or a piece of equipment permanently out of service.
examples: The Navy will *decommission* the carrier next spring.
They *decommissioned* the reactor in 2019.
The rig has been *decommissioned* and towed away.

transitivity: both — transitive (*decompress* the file), intransitive (I need to *decompress*)
gloss: To open up a compressed file, or to unwind after a stressful stretch.
examples: The app will *decompress* the archive automatically.
I *decompressed* for a week after the trial ended.
He's still *decompressing* from the move.

gloss: To break an idea, a text, or a dish down into its parts in order to examine them.
examples: Critics love to *deconstruct* his early films.
The coach *deconstructed* every play on video.
The menu features a *deconstructed* apple pie.

gloss: To remove dangerous chemicals, radiation, or germs from a place or a person.
examples: Crews *decontaminate* the suits after every shift.
They *decontaminated* the soil around the old plant.
The whole ward had to be *decontaminated*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*decouple* pay from hours), intransitive (the two markets *decoupled*)
gloss: To separate two things that used to move or work together.
examples: The proposal would *decouple* health insurance from employment.
The two markets *decoupled* for most of the year.
Emissions are slowly *decoupling* from economic growth.

gloss: To order something officially, by the authority of a ruler or a court.
examples: A president cannot simply *decree* a new tax.
The king *decreed* a day of mourning.
The judge has *decreed* that the records stay sealed.
contrast: Both e's stay: *decreed*, *decreeing*. Compare *agree — agreed — agreeing*.

gloss: To change the law so that something is no longer a crime.
examples: Several states have voted to *decriminalize* small amounts.
Portugal *decriminalized* drug possession in 2001.
Jaywalking has been *decriminalized* in California.

gloss: To condemn something publicly and strongly.
examples: Editorials *decry* the ruling almost daily.
Both parties *decried* the violence.
The mayor has been *decrying* the cuts all week.
contrast: The *-y* follows a consonant: *decries*, *decried*, but *decrying* keeps the y.

ru: передавать по дарственной, оформлять передачу собственности
gloss: To transfer property to someone by a legal document.
examples: Her parents plan to *deed* the farm to the county.
He *deeded* the house to his daughter in 1998.
The land was *deeded* to the city for a park.

transitivity: both — transitive (*deescalate* the situation), intransitive (the standoff *deescalated*)
gloss: To make a conflict or a tense situation calmer and less dangerous.
examples: Officers are trained to *deescalate* before they draw a weapon.
The talks *deescalated* the crisis for a few months.
Tensions have been *deescalating* since the ceasefire.
contrast: Usually written with a hyphen: *de-escalate*, *de-escalated*. The opposite of *escalate*.

gloss: To damage someone's reputation by saying or printing untrue things about them.
examples: You cannot *defame* a public figure without proving malice.
The paper *defamed* him and paid for it in court.
She claims she was *defamed* on the podcast.

gloss: To take away something's power to do harm.
examples: Lobbyists worked all spring to *defang* the regulation.
One amendment *defanged* the whole bill.
The committee has been *defanged* by the new rules.

ru: не выполнять обязательства, объявлять дефолт; выбираться по умолчанию
gloss: To fail to pay back a loan, or to fall back automatically on a standard option.
examples: If the country *defaults*, borrowing gets much more expensive.
He *defaulted* on two student loans.
The form kept *defaulting* to last year's address.
contrast: You *default* **on** a loan; a setting *defaults* **to** a value.

gloss: To pass solid waste out of the body.
examples: Most newborns *defecate* several times a day.
The dog *defecated* on the neighbor's lawn.
A patient who has not *defecated* in three days should call the office.
contrast: The clinical word. In conversation Americans say *poop* or *go to the bathroom*.

gloss: To spoil something clean or sacred by treating it with disrespect.
examples: Runoff from the mine *defiles* the creek every spring.
Someone *defiled* the memorial with spray paint.
The temple had been *defiled* and then abandoned.

ru: сдувать, спускать воздух; сдуваться; сбивать спесь
transitivity: both — transitive (*deflate* the tire), intransitive (the raft *deflated*)
gloss: To let the air out of something, or to make someone lose their confidence.
examples: *Deflate* the raft before you roll it up.
One comment from her *deflated* him completely.
The balloon was *deflating* faster than we could patch it.

gloss: To strip the leaves off trees and plants, usually with chemicals or insects.
examples: Gypsy moths can *defoliate* an entire hillside.
The military *defoliated* thousands of square miles of jungle.
The orchard was almost completely *defoliated* by June.

gloss: To cut down all the trees over a large area.
examples: Cattle ranching *deforests* more land than logging does.
Settlers *deforested* the valley within a generation.
Much of the basin has already been *deforested*.

transitivity: both — transitive (heat *deforms* the plastic), intransitive (the frame *deformed*)
gloss: To change the shape of something so that it is bent or spoiled.
examples: Heat will *deform* the plastic housing.
The impact *deformed* the front wheel.
The beams were *deforming* under the weight of the snow.

gloss: To pay part or all of someone's costs.
examples: The grant helps *defray* travel expenses.
A bake sale *defrayed* most of the cost of the trip.
Tuition is partly *defrayed* by the scholarship.
contrast: The *-y* follows a vowel, so it stays: *defrays*, *defrayed*. Compare *carry — carried*.

gloss: To remove a priest or minister from the clergy as a punishment.
examples: The church can *defrock* a priest without a criminal trial.
The diocese *defrocked* him in 2004.
Two *defrocked* priests testified at the hearing.

gloss: To stop providing money to an organization or a program.
examples: Congress threatened to *defund* the agency.
The state *defunded* the program in 2011.
Arts education has been quietly *defunded* for years.

gloss: To get steadily worse, or to sink into a lower and uglier state.
examples: These meetings always *degenerate* into shouting.
The debate *degenerated* within ten minutes.
His eyesight has been *degenerating* since the surgery.
contrast: The verb ends in -rayt; the adjective and noun end in a schwa: dih-JEN-uh-ruht. Usually *degenerate into* something.

gloss: To pour liquid into a hot pan to loosen the browned bits and make a sauce.
examples: *Deglaze* the pan with a splash of white wine.
She *deglazed* the skillet with stock and poured it over the meat.
*Deglazing* takes about thirty seconds.
contrast: You *deglaze* a pan **with** wine, stock, or water.

gloss: To treat or portray people as though they were not human beings.
examples: Propaganda works by *dehumanizing* the other side.
The system *dehumanized* everyone who passed through it.
Prisoners described being *dehumanized* by the daily routine.

gloss: To remove moisture from the air in a room or a building.
examples: A small unit will *dehumidify* the whole basement.
We *dehumidified* the crawl space before laying the floor.
The machine has been *dehumidifying* for two days.

ru: очищать ото льда, обрабатывать противообледенительным составом
gloss: To remove ice from a surface, especially an aircraft or a windshield.
examples: Crews *deice* the wings right before takeoff.
They *deiced* the plane twice and we still missed our slot.
The runway is being *deiced* now.

gloss: To treat a person or a thing as if it were a god.
examples: Fans *deify* a coach after one good season.
Rome *deified* several of its emperors.
He has been *deified* by an industry that once ignored him.

gloss: To do something you consider beneath you, as though it were a favor.
examples: He won't even *deign* to answer the email.
She finally *deigned* to look up from her phone.
They have never *deigned* to explain the decision.
contrast: The *g* is silent: DAYN, like *Dane*. Almost always *deign to do* something.

gloss: To make an institution, a leader, or a result seem not legitimate.
examples: Endless lawsuits *delegitimize* the whole process.
The broadcast *delegitimized* the election in the eyes of millions.
The court has been *delegitimized* by the fight over appointments.

gloss: To describe or mark out something clearly and in detail.
examples: The contract should *delineate* each party's duties.
The treaty *delineated* the border river by river.
Responsibilities are carefully *delineated* in the handbook.

ru: исключать из списка, снимать с биржевых торгов
gloss: To remove a company from a stock exchange, or an item from an official list.
examples: The exchange can *delist* a stock that trades under a dollar.
Nasdaq *delisted* the company in March.
The species was *delisted* once the population recovered.

gloss: To make someone believe something that is not true.
examples: Don't *delude* yourself about the numbers.
He *deluded* investors for six years.
They were *deluded* into thinking the job was safe.

gloss: To take the magnetism out of something.
examples: A phone case can *demagnetize* a hotel key.
The scanner *demagnetized* my credit card.
The strip has been *demagnetized*, so you'll need a new card.

gloss: To mark or fix the boundary between two things or areas.
examples: Orange cones *demarcate* the work zone.
The treaty *demarcated* the two territories in 1904.
The two roles are not clearly *demarcated*.

gloss: To remove armed forces and weapons from an area.
examples: Both sides agreed to *demilitarize* the border.
The islands were *demilitarized* after the war.
They are *demilitarizing* the zone one checkpoint at a time.

gloss: To show how a product works by using it in front of people.
examples: She'll *demo* the new release at the conference.
They *demoed* the app for us over lunch.
We've been *demoing* the machine in stores all month.
contrast: The o stays in every form: *demos*, *demoed*, *demoing*.

transitivity: both — transitive (*demobilize* the troops), intransitive (the militia *demobilized*)
gloss: To send soldiers home and take an army out of active service.
examples: The agreement requires both armies to *demobilize*.
Washington *demobilized* millions of men in 1945.
Fighters are being *demobilized* under UN supervision.

gloss: To give far more people access to something, or to make a country democratic.
examples: Cheap cameras *democratize* filmmaking.
The reforms *democratized* the party's nominating process.
Access to data has been *democratized* by these tools.

ru: демонетизировать, лишать возможности зарабатывать; изымать из обращения
gloss: To stop a video or a channel from earning money, or to take a banknote out of circulation.
examples: Platforms *demonetize* videos that mention certain topics.
India *demonetized* its two largest banknotes in 2016.
Her whole channel was *demonetized* overnight.

gloss: To portray a person or a group as evil.
examples: Campaigns *demonize* whoever is easiest to blame.
The coverage *demonized* an entire neighborhood.
Immigrants have been *demonized* in every recession.

gloss: To take away someone's confidence, hope, or willingness to keep going.
examples: Long shifts and no raise *demoralize* even good nurses.
The loss *demoralized* the whole team.
The staff is completely *demoralized*.

gloss: To move someone to a lower rank or position.
examples: They may *demote* him rather than fire him.
The league *demoted* two officials after the review.
He was *demoted* to a desk job in March.

gloss: To make someone lose interest in working or trying.
examples: Nothing *demotivates* a team faster than a pointless meeting.
The new quota *demotivated* half the sales floor.
Students are *demotivated* by grading they don't understand.

ru: возражать, выражать несогласие; уклоняться от ответа
gloss: To object politely, or to hesitate rather than agree.
examples: Two board members *demur* whenever the topic comes up.
She *demurred* when reporters asked about the money.
He was still *demurring* an hour into the negotiation.
contrast: The r doubles: *demurred*, *demurring*. Not the adjective *demure* (dih-MYOOR, 'modest and quiet').

gloss: To make a difficult or mysterious subject easy to understand.
examples: The book tries to *demystify* the tax code.
Her lecture *demystified* the whole process.
He spends his weekends *demystifying* statistics for beginners.

transitivity: both — transitive (heat *denatures* the protein), intransitive (the enzyme *denatured*)
gloss: To change the natural structure of a protein, or to make alcohol unfit to drink.
examples: Heat and acid both *denature* egg proteins.
The sample *denatured* at seventy degrees.
Industrial alcohol is *denatured* so that nobody will drink it.

gloss: To criticize someone or something unfairly in order to make them seem worthless.
examples: He never *denigrates* his competitors in public.
The review *denigrated* the entire genre.
Her work was *denigrated* for years before anyone reconsidered it.

gloss: To be a sign of something, or to stand for it.
examples: In this table an asterisk *denotes* an estimate.
The red line *denoted* the old border.
The suffix has always *denoted* something small.
contrast: *Denote* is what a word or sign literally stands for; *connote* is what it suggests.

gloss: To strip a place bare of its covering, especially of plants or soil.
examples: Overgrazing can *denude* a hillside in a single season.
Logging *denuded* the ridge above the town.
The slopes had been *denuded* long before the flood.

gloss: To be decided by something else, or to rely on someone for support.
examples: How long it takes *depends* on the weather.
The whole town *depended* on one factory.
Thousands of families are *depending* on that check.

gloss: To get off an airplane.
examples: Passengers in rows twenty and up may *deplane* now.
We *deplaned* on the tarmac in the rain.
They were still *deplaning* when our flight started boarding.
contrast: Airline English. In conversation Americans say *get off the plane*.

gloss: To say strongly and publicly that you think something is very wrong.
examples: We *deplore* the use of force against protesters.
The statement *deplored* the attack but named no one.
Such language has been *deplored* by every previous chair.

gloss: To greatly reduce the number of people living in a place.
examples: Factory closures can *depopulate* a small town in a decade.
War and famine *depopulated* the province.
Whole counties have been *depopulated* since the 1980s.

ru: свергать, смещать; снимать показания под присягой
gloss: To remove a ruler from power, or to question a witness under oath before a trial.
examples: Generals rarely *depose* a leader without foreign help.
The army *deposed* the president in 1973.
Both executives have already been *deposed* by the plaintiffs' lawyers.

ru: не одобрять, осуждать; объявлять устаревшим (в IT)
gloss: To express disapproval of something, or to mark a software feature as outdated.
examples: Most style guides *deprecate* this construction.
The team *deprecated* the old API last spring.
That function has been *deprecated* — use the new one.
contrast: Not *depreciate*, which is about losing value. Note *self-deprecating*, 'making fun of oneself'.

transitivity: both — transitive (*depreciate* the equipment), intransitive (a new car *depreciates*)
gloss: To fall in value over time, or to write down the value of an asset.
examples: A new car starts to *depreciate* the moment you drive it off the lot.
The peso *depreciated* sharply against the dollar.
The equipment is being *depreciated* over five years.
contrast: *Depreciate* is about value; *deprecate* is about disapproval.

transitivity: both — transitive (*depressurize* the tank), intransitive (the cabin *depressurized*)
gloss: To release the pressure inside a sealed container or an aircraft cabin.
examples: Technicians *depressurize* the tank before opening it.
The cabin *depressurized* at thirty thousand feet.
The chamber is slowly *depressurizing*.

gloss: To treat something as less important than it was before.
examples: Let's *deprioritize* the redesign until after launch.
Management *deprioritized* the whole feature.
Maintenance has been *deprioritized* for three budget cycles.

gloss: To free someone from beliefs that a cult or a movement pushed on them.
examples: Families sometimes hire specialists to *deprogram* a relative.
It took two years to *deprogram* him.
She writes about being *deprogrammed* in the 1980s.

transitivity: both — transitive (the sheriff *deputized* them), intransitive (he *deputized* for the chair)
gloss: To give someone official power to act for you, especially as a deputy.
examples: A sheriff can *deputize* ordinary citizens in an emergency.
He *deputized* two ranchers to help with the search.
The volunteers were *deputized* that same afternoon.

gloss: To remove government rules from an industry.
examples: Both parties promised to *deregulate* small banks.
Congress *deregulated* the airlines in 1978.
Trucking has been *deregulated* for decades.

gloss: To speak about someone or something with open contempt.
examples: Critics *deride* the plan as a giveaway.
Reviewers *derided* the film when it came out.
The idea was *derided* for years and then quietly adopted.
contrast: Often *deride something* **as** something: *derided it as a stunt*.

gloss: To remove the salt from seawater so that it can be used or drunk.
examples: The plant can *desalinate* fifty million gallons a day.
Israel *desalinated* its way out of a water crisis.
Most of the city's water is now *desalinated*.

gloss: To damage or show great disrespect for a holy or honored place.
examples: It is a felony to *desecrate* a grave.
Someone *desecrated* the synagogue over the weekend.
The chapel had been *desecrated* during the occupation.

gloss: To end the legal separation of racial groups in schools or public places.
examples: The ruling ordered the district to *desegregate*.
Little Rock *desegregated* Central High in 1957.
Many school systems were never fully *desegregated*.

gloss: To remove something from a set of selected items, usually by clicking it again.
examples: *Deselect* every box except the first one.
I *deselected* the photos I didn't want.
Nothing happens until all the layers are *deselected*.

gloss: To make someone or something less sensitive or less easily affected.
examples: Violent images can *desensitize* young viewers.
Years of coverage *desensitized* the public.
Patients are gradually *desensitized* to the allergen.

gloss: To dry something out completely.
examples: A hot wind can *desiccate* a field in two days.
The drought *desiccated* the whole valley.
The recipe calls for *desiccated* coconut.

gloss: To officially choose something for a purpose, or to give it a name or a status.
examples: The city will *designate* two blocks as a historic district.
Congress *designated* the area a national monument in 1996.
He has been *designated* as the acting director.
contrast: Here the *g* is pronounced: DEZ-ig-nayt — unlike *design*, dih-ZYN.
